The Matoran text on the Coliseum balcony reads: "Sidorak king of the Visorak".

Two Lohrak beasts swoop over the Toa Metru for a very brief moment at the beginning of the film. According to the directors, they were supposed to appear as enemies in the previous movie, Bionicle 2: Legends of Metru Nui, but because of time restrains, had to be cut. A herd of Kikanalo beasts from the second movie and a worm-like Kraata serpent from the first one can also be seen in this scene. Also, the birds flying away from the Coliseum balcony at Sidorak's approach recycle the animation model of Nivawk, also from the second movie. They are not, however, supposed to be members of the same bird species.

At one point in the film, Vakama gets attacked by a Muaka - a large tiger-like Rahi (Bionicle animal). The beast depicted here bears no resemblance to the Muaka toy, and is actually a barely modified CG model of Graalok, the Ash Bear from the first Bionicle movie. The Muaka in toy form has tracks instead of hind legs and an extremely long, expandable neck, while the Muaka that appears in the movie does not. Although it can be assumed that this particular Muaka has been mutated by the Visorak spiders' venom, and is thus a Muaka Hordika, not a "normal" Muaka tiger.

Roodaka's name means "treachery" in Matoran (the main Bionicle language used during its first story). It earned this meaning for her treacherous and manipulative behavior that we see in the movie, and also for her being a double-agent for the Brotherhood of Makuta and the Dark Hunters (two of the most powerful Bionicle organizations).

SPOILER: The main female antagonist, Roodaka has a really vague fate. In the movie, we see her falling to the ground, lying motionless. Then a shadow-hand emerges from the heart-stone in her chest, grabs her body, and makes it disappear. None of the characters note what actually happened to her, and she is totally forgotten for the rest of the film. In fact, the Bionicle fans have believed that Roodaka died, and would never appear in any other Bionicle media. This assumption has been false, and the return of Roodaka in later Bionicle story-lines proves this. So what happened to her in the movie? Story writer Greg Farshtey tells us the answer: "Makuta spirited her out of harms way". Which means that Roodaka didn't really die, she was basically knocked unconscious. The shadow-hand that we see in the film belongs to the villainous Makuta Teridax, using one of his many powers to teleport her away from the heroes.

In the companion book and an early version of the script, Roodaka talks to the captured Makuta by riding a mutated Nui-Kopen (a kind of giant wasp) out to the sea to the body of Makuta. In the film however, she simply talks to a stone representing Makuta inside her chamber. Whether because of technical or financial difficulties or time restrains, the Nui-Kopen ride had to be neglected, but according to story writer 'Greg Farshtey', it is still considered to be canon.

The Rahaga characters' bodies were lifted straight from the animation models of the Turaga from _Bionicle: Mask of Light (2003) (V)_ (qv), while their feet were borrowed from the main Matoran characters of _Bionicle 2: Legends of Metru Nui (2004) (V)_ (qv). Their head is that of a Rahkshi, however since the Rahkshi that appeared in the movies have very alien looking heads that split apart, the designers made them look much more closer to the toys' heads, so that they could emote better.

An earlier version of the script describes a humorous scene that was cut from the movie. In this scene, Matau tries to build a nest, showcasing his animal side taking over. This sequence was included in the movie novel.

At the beginning of the kohli match, the competitors salute each other by saying "play well." Lego, the company that produces the Bionicle toys, takes its name from the Danish phrase "leg godt", which means "play well".

Though the Bionicle toys had been around for several years by the time of this film's release, the characters were designed to look as if they inspired the toys, rather than being inspired by them: while the animators could have recreated the exact look of the toys, they gave the characters a more biological look.

And, in fact, several of the creatures in the film, including Pewku the crab and the gukko bird, actually were the inspiration for the toys - the film versions came first, with the Lego designers creating the toys based loosely on the animators' work.

At the end of the credits, a small message in Bionicle symbols can be seen. It translates to "No Rahi (Bionicle animals) were harmed during the making of this film." This is a reference to when Jaller is about to kill Graalok the Ash Bear but Lewa stops him.

After Takua alerts the people of Onu-Koro with the news that Rahkshi have attacked him, Toa Pohatu responds by asking "What is Rahkshi?". In the Bionicle lore, it is a running joke that after hearing a name or expression for the first time, Pohatu always asks what it means. Usually, though, he doesn't get straight answers from any of the other characters.

When Lewa Nuva asks Takua and Jaller if they've ever flown a Gukko bird, Takua states that he has "been a second but never flown one himself". He is referring to the 'Mata Nui Online Game', an online flash-game from the initial year of Bionicle, where the player had to complete different tasks and go on various adventures in the shoes of Takua - one of them was being a second on a Gukko bird (albeit on a different sub-species of Gukko).

According to the directors' commentary track on the DVD, the first scene of the entire film, in which stones are used to introduce the viewers to the Bionicle myth and explain the basic knowledge, was in fact the last scene to be animated and a last-minute addition.

The only movie of the first Bionicle trilogy to be centered around half a year's storyline. Its two sequels had to squeeze in plot points of one year's worth of Bionicle story, and as a result, there is a big gap in both of them, with lots of events happening off-screen. Because of this, not many aspects of the story and, more importantly, only a fraction of the characters' character development could be covered. In this respect, this movie is the "cleanest" of the three.

Although it is hard to see because of the lighting, Makuta Teridax actually pulls out the Kraata worms of his own body to put them into their suits of amour, and doesn't simply pick them up from the floor of his lair.

All the background Matoran seen in the movie only wear five types of masks: Komau (the type of mask Turaga Onewa wears), Kakama (the same kind of mask Hewkii is seen wearing), Ruru (Turaga Whenua and Hafu), Rau (Turaga Nokam), and Huna (Turaga Vakama and Macku). The Hau, Kaukau, and Pakari are exclusive to only Hahli, Jaller, and Takua. Of the six major Matoran tribes, only the members of four appear in the film (fire, stone, water, and earth), while Matoran of Ice and Air are absent. Takua is a special case: he is a Matoran of Light, although at the time this movie was made, he was still considered a fire Matoran. Finally, of the island's six districts, only Ta-Wahi (fire), Le-Wahi (air), Ko-Wahi (ice), and Onu-Wahi (earth) are seen, with Ga-Wahi (water) and Po-Wahi (stone) being absent from the movie.

The behavior of Takua in this movie contradicts his earlier portrayals from other media. Namely, his strong sense of responsibility and duty seem to be missing, and he also appears to be more lazy and reckless, less confident.
The head design of Graalok the Ash Bear was heavily based on the mask of Lewa Nuva, the Toa of Air, with strongly tweaked proportions.

Originally the first scene of Makuta's lair was to be longer. He would have talked about his former plans to gain control over the island, explaining some of the Bionicle story leading up to that point. But the scene didn't move the plot forward, and it gave away the appearances of the menacing Rahkhsi too early, so they scrapped it.

A very early concept for this movie would have taken a completely different route than the finished product. Apparently a human child, live acted, would have somehow gotten into the Bionicle universe, and he would have become the Seventh Toa, rather than an actual Bionicle character. This idea must have gotten scrapped quite early in the movie's development, since apart from a handful of instances of LEGO employees (like the Bionicle story writer, Gregory Farshtey, who was otherwise not directly involved with the movie) mentioning it, nothing is known about it. But it has been accepted as a fact by now that the real world and the Bionicle world do not co-exist, therefor we wouldn't be seeing any humans in the storyline.

The torso of the female Toa, Gali, was originally designed to be an upside-down version of those of her male partners, much like that of the infamous Pohatu and Pohatu Nuva toy (who is male). Although in the end, she received a right side-up variation, she retained some design elements from the upside-down torso, like the multiple metal panels on her stomach. To make her look even more feminine, they added a feature to her feet, namely the ability to turn high-heeled.

The story writer and former Bionicle Story Team leader 'Bob Thompson (VII)' (qv) is said to have made strange Rahkshi sounds with his mouth during production. The team later opted to create a brand new sound for them to be used in the movie, but the directors said Bob himself could have voiced them just as well.

Directors 'David Molina (I)' (qv) and 'Terry Shakespeare' (qv) are huge 'Ray Harryhausen' (qv) fans, and the way movie's villains, Makuta and the Rahkshi move in certain shots reflects the choppy movements of stop-motion animated characters.

In the audio commentary for the movie, the directors talk about how they initially envisioned the characters with the power to transform their hands into tools, so that they could interact with objects and each other, but also resemble their toy counterparts. It turned out, however, that the plot never made this decision necessary, so they abandoned the idea, and instead gave the characters regular hands, and separate tools.

Most of the action scenes were deleted in the German release of the movie, along with nearly all the shots of the Rahkshi opening their heads and the introduction scene for the first "batch" of Rahkshi. This is because in Germany, the movie had to be marketed towards a younger audience, and these scenes were considered too frightening.

The animators went to great lengths to make the movie characters look as close to their toy counterparts as they can. In the first three Miramax-produced Bionicle animated movies, muscle and flesh were added to the otherwise mechanical looking characters, and some of their other features have been tweaked as well to make them look more like living beings, rather then robots (they were given fingers and mouths, for example). That is not the case in this movie - the characters even have the pins and axles showing that keep their bodies together, and they also wear a life-counter gear, something that was originally meant to be a toy-only feature. But to be able to emote better, their helmets can retract the parts that cover their mouths, and eyebrows were also added to them.

Even though the Bionicle characters that appear in this movie are 85% organic and only 15% of their bodies is actually mechanical, all the characters look like fully mechanical robots. They designed them this way intentionally. The little Scarabax beetles however do look mostly organic.
The planet of Bara Magna and its two moons, along with the two dagger-like curved "swooshes" of space-dust on both sides represent the Bionicle symbol of Unity, Duty, and Destiny.

The random background Agori villagers were made to look exactly the same as the toy figures of the six main Agori. The village leaders, however, were given large shoulder pads to make viewers able to tell them apart. This way you can see the differences between Raanu (a village leader) and a "normal" Fire Agori, Metus and an Ice Agori, and Berix and his village's leader. The leader of the Jungle Tribe (unnamed) also seems to have regular four-fingered hands rather than the three huge claws the normal Jungle Agori have.

In the movie, the Ice Tribe Glatorian Strakk is seen carrying the shield of Metus, another member of the Ice Tribe, while Ackar of the Fire Tribe has Raanu's shield, who is the Fire Tribe's leader. This is because their toys don't feature secondary defensive equipment, and the script required them to use these.

The reason as to why the characters use Thornax launchers so sparsely in the movie is because the design of the launchers had not been finalized yet when the production has already began. The ammunition is also depicted as explosive, glowing orbs crackling with energy, rather than the simple round, spiky and rarely explosive fruits that we see in the comics and books.

If you observe the gigantic four-legged Skopio creature closely, you can notice what look like yellow Bionicle arms in the side of its head, along its neck, and another yellow, oval-shaped "head" on the back of its neck. These "arms" and the "head" come from the Skopio XV-1 building set, on which the creature was based. The toy however represents a mechanical robot Skopio, rather than a living one, and has a yellow pilot controlling it, named Telluris. The yellow arms and head on the movie Skopio are thus his body parts, made to look like they belong to the Skopio's anatomy, since Telluris isn't sitting on it, and is in fact not even a movie character. The rest of Telluris' body, like his legs, seem to be hidden away inside the Skopio's design, proving the notion that what looks like him was indeed meant to be one with the Skopio. This caused quite a bit of head-scratching to the fans, but there is a reason for this interesting design choice. Namely, without Telluris, the Skopio model looks hollow and empty, not to mention skinny. The designers had to build Telluris' parts into it to make it look more bulky, more like a living creature.

Although the fourth Bionicle movie overall, the title doesn't have a number in it. This is most likely because the first three movies have been made by a different studio (Miramax, rather than Universal), by different people, and because their stories do not tie in strongly with the new movie's.

The portrayal of the Glatorian character named Gresh in this movie differs greatly from his earlier appearances in the Bionicle book and comic series that take place before the movie's story. In those, he acts maturely and seriously for his age, and in the movie he acts much more childishly. This is the direct opposite of what viewers are used to, as usually immature characters become mature in the course of a story. However all the comics and books were written when the movie's script had already been finished, meaning that the way Gresh acts in the movie is what his creators originally intended him to behave like. The in-story explanation for this is that Gresh learned to be more bright and less serious with the help of his hot-headed but playful female friend Kiina, who acts just as juvenile in some scenes.

The idea to make Click, Mata Nui's companion Scarabax beetle, have the ability to turn into a shield for his master at will was the idea of director 'Mark Baldo' (qv). It was not originally in the script, but story writer Greg Farshtey thought it was a cute idea so he approved it.
The name of the desert planet Bara Magna means "Great Barren".

Some main characters that did not make it into the movie are Malum, a former Glatorian of the Fire Village, now banished into the desert and Gelu, former Glatorian of the Ice Village, now a caravan guard. Although they have played important roles in the story set before the movie, they had to be left out of it, simply because there were already enough characters to focus on.

The identity of the Agori traitor was kept under tight wraps prior to the movie. No one could be informed about it, not even the comic artists, which is why the traitor character appeared as a dark, unrecognizable figure, cloaked in shadows in one of the comics, with (incorrect) glowing red eyes.
The giant monster that the united Scarabax beetles form uses the animation model of Malum, a character that was left out of the movie. This is his cameo.
During the fight with the Skopio beast, you can clearly hear it making Godzilla's distinctive roar.

WILHELM SCREAM: As the Bone Hunters get trapped under the falling rocks, you can hear it. (What's strange about this is that in this movie, Bone Hunters are shown to be able to produce only grunts and growls, and thus the Wilhelm scream stands out awkwardly.)

The walls of the secret laboratory of the Great Beings are covered with Bionicle writing. Some interesting words can be read, these include: "LEGO", "Mata Nui", "Bara Magna", "secret lab", "Threshold" (the studio that produced the movie), "Universal", "Bionicle the legend", "2009", "CGCG". "Mata Nui robot" is written over the blueprints of said robot, and the words "heart chamber" point to its chest, while "Bara Magna test site" is written next to it.

The various shields that cover Ackar's wall are familiar Bionicle LEGO pieces. Fans might recognize Axonn's blade, Nuparu Mahri's shield, Metus' shield, Gahlok-Kal's Magnetism Shield, and an often used armor piece from the 2008 toys.

The Matoran we see inside Mata Nui's original body all wear only two kinds of masks, Noble Mirus and Noble Kakamas. This was probably a decision made to cut corners, as the animators had to design fewer masks this way.

The sequence where a horde of intrigued Scarabax beetles are wandering through the desert and stumble upon a new arrival, Toa Mata Nui (in the form of a mask that has just crash-landed) and witness his rebirth is very similar to the first scene of the first Bionicle comic book, where a group of Ussal crabs can be seen gathering around the coastline where the capsule carrying Toa Kopaka has been washed ashore and watch as he builds his bodyparts back together.

SPOILER: Due to a faulty script or directing, Tuma's fate is never cleared. When we last see him, he is lying motionless on the ground, with his eyes gone black and he is gone from the rest of the movie. He is in fact alive.

Even though one might think that, due to his voice and the way he speaks, Gresh is the youngest Glatorian of the movie, it is in fact noble and deep-voiced Mata Nui, being "only" a hundred thousand years old. Gresh was already around by the time Mata Nui came into being.

After the creators of the movie referred to its characters as "giant robots" in interviews, and had shown evidence in the movie itself that they might very well believe them to be robots (making them look fully mechanical, adding servo sounds to their movements and making them spark), some fans have voiced their doubts that the staff was aware of one of Bionicle's first and foremost fact: that most of its characters are not robots, rather biomechanical creatures. This has lead to some fans ridiculing them in non-offensive ways.

The end of the movie does not conclude the plot and is left wide open. This was probably done as a response to the recent changes in the Bionicle toy and storyline and the plans to end it. Since the creators of the movie didn't know how well it would be received and how the story might continue, they left the ending vague on purpose. This way they wouldn't have needed to continue it directly from where it had finished, and they could have simply jumped over a full story arc for the next movie, which could have thus concentrated on the conclusion of the Bionicle story line, rather than on a side-plot. The LEGO Corporation however has, during production, axed the Bionicle toy-line, which sealed the fate of the planned movie-trilogy. No sequel will be made.

Bionicle story writer 'Gregory Farshtey' has claimed that he wasn't aware of some of the decisions made by the movie staff after he had approved of the script. This is probably the reason why a portion of the fanbase feels that the movie seems to be so different from what they had expected. Also, this explains all the storyline inconsistencies seen in the movie.

Originally, the beast that attacks Mata Nui upon his arrival was to be attacked and eaten by the Scarabax beetles. This idea was obviously dropped, probably to give the beetles a better chance to shine, and it also would have been too violent for a children's movie.

The Bone Hunters in the movie do not look like their toy figures. Instead, the are identical to their relatives, the Rock Tribe Agori, and all look exactly the same as the Atakus toy figure. This is because when the animation models were designed, the Bone Hunter prototypes still looked like Atakus. The final models however received a different look, but there was no time to correct it for the movie.

A rough draft for the sequel was written before the LEGO Corporation decided to axe the Bionicle line of toys, and thus any chance of new, official movies being made. However since the rights haven't been bought by anyone, the draft could be freely shared online, and story writer 'Gregory Farshtey' uploaded it onto his blog. This way the fans could see what direction the story would have taken. Like this movie, the never-to-be-made sequel would have ended with a huge cliffhanger, clearly indicating that a third installment was also planned. As thing stand, though, no official continuation will be made in movie form.
The character Kiina was originally to have a heavy Russian accent.
The first draft of the script had a quicksand scene in it. Due to animation difficulties, it had to be cut.
Kiina's name was based off the name of story writer Greg Farshtey's wife, Jackina.
Mata Nui mentions to Ackar that he reminds him of a Toa hero he once knew. According to the backstory, he was thinking of Toa Onua, who appeared in _Bionicle: Mask of Light (2003) (V)_ (qv).

The novel accompanying the movie was written before the finalized script, and thus tells us what the movie makers originally had in mind for certain scenes. A couple of interesting things to note: Mata Nui was originally gold and white instead of gold and black, and when Click transformed into a shield, only one of his eyes remained, instead of his whole face, as we see in the movie. Some scenes are also described differently. For instance, the Vorox broke off its tail by smashing it into a rock, rather than into Mata Nui's shield. It is also worth noting that the book tells us why the characters behave the way they do (the otherwise grim Kiina is cheerful because she doesn't want Mata Nui to know how terrible their lives are, and some of the things she tells him are actually blatant lies), and that most of the slapstick comedy moments are also absent. Finally, the novel mentions Bionicle characters and places (like Certavus and Iconox) that are never spoken of in the movie, and also explains plot points better (like why the Glatorian all stay in the village of Tesara).

The sword that Mata Nui uses, as well as the Glatorians' old weapons are not based on existing LEGO pieces, which is unusual, considering their importance and that the main driving force behind the movie was to promote the toys. The character Berix also lacks the accessories his toy comes with (his shield, sword, and the flexible tube that connects to his back). Most likely, his animation model was designed and completed before his toy.

The creators of the movie did consider hiring the composer for the first three Bionicle movies, 'Nathan Furst' (qv) to write the musical score, but instead went with 'John D'Andrea (I)' (qv), claiming they wanted a "clean start" to separate the movie from the other trilogy.

In supplementary story materials, like the comic or novel adaptation (which were written according to early drafts), the characters made a point of stating the fighter Strakk will be banished to the wastelands for his behavior in the arena. The final script removed all references to this act, thus Strakk seemingly walks away without being punished.

The director, Toni Harman, was inspired to make "Doula! The Ultimate Birth Companion" following her own difficult birth experience which ended in an emergency caesarean. This was before she knew about doulas and the film was made as a reaction to her experience, to explore whether a doula would have made a difference.
The cast and crew were mostly sophomores at Temple University when Downhill was made.
Downhill was shot in 11 days and had 2 days of re-shoots.
SPOILER: In the scene where Jonah and Teddy kill Cal, who has a jacket draped over his head, the cinematographer, 'Jason Rihaly' (qv), doubled for 'Kyle Martin (IX)' (qv).
'Melissa Phan (II)' (qv) happened to be enrolled in a rock climbing class with 'Joe Gariffo' (qv) which ultimately led to her being cast as Rachel.

Tyrone's line to Jonah: "You're nothing compared to people like me. You are dog shit!" was originally scripted as: "You're nothing compared to people like me. You are scrapple!" The line was inexplicably changed at the last minute. Jonah's response was thus changed from: "Scrapple tastes good!" to "Dog shit tastes good!"
The entire cast performed their own stunts.
The soapbox cars broke down on a regular basis delaying the filming of the climactic race scenes until the latter half of the shoot.
Following the success of 'Downhill', the cast and crew were set to begin production on a film entitled 'Escape from Zombie Island' but the film is currently stuck in developmental hell.

'Alex Lees' (qv) (Ben) showed up on set one day dressed in a Green Lantern costume. The crew decided to shoot a quick scene where he tackles a random student while Jonah, Teddy, and their friends converse in the school cafeteria oblivious to what's going on behind them. The scene was included in the final cut of the film.
'Zac Caruolo' (qv) (Tim) was originally scripted to die in the finale, but the idea was eventually scrapped.
Director 'Shane Bissett' (qv) was the only crew member present when shooting the scene where Jonah and Dana share a kiss in Dana's bedroom.
The lines spoken by 'Frank Coralluzzo' (qv) and 'Alex Lees' (qv) in the 'Hip Cool Bastards' scene were completely ad-libbed.

'Don Manigly (I)' (qv) kept begging director 'Shane Bissett' (qv) to give his character additional screen time while 'Tom Milewski (I)' (qv) (Mitch Delaney)wanted to have his screen time reduced. Both actors' requests were ultimately granted.

The crew had great difficulty finding an actress to play Dana's grandmother. At one point, someone suggested dressing 'Mario Maiale' (qv) (Tyrone) in drag, but this was deemed far too hokey. Eventually, one of 'Joe Gariffo' (qv)'s elderly neighbors, Ray Testa, agreed to play the role despite having no prior acting experience.

'Chris Galanti' (qv)'s dad makes an appearance as Teddy's dad, while 'Joe Gariffo' (qv)'s dad plays a security guard that throws Jonah off of school property. 'Frank Coralluzzo's parents play Jonah's parents.

The climactic showdown in the woods was originally scripted to be an epic gunfight. When the crew realized that the sounds of gunfire might cause a disturbance in the neighborhood where they were filming, the scene was rewritten to be more of a street fight, complete with footballs, bats, swords, etc.
Writer/Director 'Shane Bissett' (qv) makes a cameo appearance in the infamous 'basement' scene where Tim and his friends plot to kill Jonah.
'Don Manigly (I)' (qv) was considered for the roles of Zach and John before being cast as 'Don'. His character's name was Jason in the original script.
The roles of Jonah and Teddy were always intended for Joe Gariffo and 'Chris Galanti' (qv).
In the first draft of the script, the show Teddy was obsessed with was _"M*A*S*H" (1972)_ (qv), not '"MacGyver" (1985)'.
'Joe Mcfadden' (qv), who plays the school counselor, is a co-worker of 'Joe Gariffo' (qv)'s father, the security guard.
'Joe Gariffo' (qv)'s mother was also slated to play Dana's grandmother at one point, but she was offended when she was offered the role.

The episode of _"MacGyver"_ that Jonah and Dana watch together is not an actual episode from the series. The filmmakers would've needed to get legal permission to use footage from the series so they came up with a compromise. 'Shane Bissett' (qv) recorded all new lines of dialogue and inserted new sound effects to make it seem like Jonah and Dana were watching a real episode of MacGyver when they, in fact, were not.
Based on characters from the TV series _"Doctor Who" (1963)_ (qv).
_Dracula II: Ascension (2003) (V)_ (qv) and this movie were shot together as one movie. It was the director's and producers' intention to split the film into two during the shooting.
Visual Effects were done half in Bulgaria, and half in California.
The split screens were added in the edit as an attempt to make the "talking heads" scenes more interesting.
Entire video was conceived, filmed and edited in Santa Ana, California on the campus of the Art Institute of California-Orange County in January-February-March 2007.

The scene where Drake destroys the mill by accident is partly re-used from _DragonHeart (1996)_ (qv) when Bowen and Draco attacked the first village - footage from the first film is used as the mill bursts into flames.
Drake is the only film dragon that can breath ice..

The novel "Dragons of Autumn Twilight" is the first book in the Dragonlance Chronicles trilogy. The Chronicles are the first trilogy in the series of Dragonlance novels and anthologies that now number close to 150 books, several of which were on the New York Times Bestseller List.

In the mid-1990s, the Jim Henson Company was in talks with TSR, which was the owner of Dungeons and Dragons and also Dragonlance, to produce some type of Dragonlance project. However when TSR was bought out by Wizards of the Coast, the project was dropped.

'Kiefer Sutherland' (qv) actually looked into the whole background of his character, Raistlin, before showing up on the set to do the recording. He was continuously worried about the pronunciation of the magic spells, so they had to to record multiple takes around his spell casting.
Due to the small budget, getting 'Kiefer Sutherland' (qv) to play the voice of Raistlin was a long shot and not really expected to the production crew until the day he said he would do it.

Director 'J.L. Carrozza' (qv) credits a story he once heard of a girl's guardian angel saving her from a rapist who was stalking her as the influence behind the story of this film. Other heavy influences included _Straw Dogs (1971)_ (qv) and a Chinese horror film called _The Other World_.

As with his previous film _Little Red Riding Hood (2009/I) (V)_ (qv), this was made with money entirely from the pocket of director 'J.L. Carrozza' (qv), shot on a Canon GL2 borrowed from 'Neil Cicierega' (qv) which was also used to shoot Cicierega's _Potter Puppet Pals: The Mysterious Ticking Noise_, one of the most popular viral internet videos of all time. The film was shot entirely in and around Plymouth County, Massachusetts and the actors, some of whom also appeared in _Little Red Riding Hood_ were all local non-professionals who appeared in the film for free and many of them, especially 'David Luce (III)' (qv), provided their own props and costumes.

One of the biggest influences on the film was director 'Mario Bava' (qv). 'J.L. Carrozza' (qv) watched _I tre volti della paura (1963)_ (qv) and several of his other films numerous times during production. The titular dream house's address is "334 Bava Ave".

Shot nearly concurrently with _No Place Like Home_, a 2007 _Wizard of Oz (1939)_ parody directed by 'Ryan Murphy (XVII)' (qv). During that summer, some days and weeks would be devoted to _No Place Like Home_, others to _Dream House_. 'Kevin James (XIV)' (qv), who plays Gary here, was also shooting a comedy film entitled _Hip Hop Cherry Pop_.
Poet 'Mike Amado' (qv), who played one of the "townies", passed away early in 2009. He was only 33.

Director 'J.L. Carrozza' (qv) was very unhappy with the 26 minute edit of the film and redid the film in early 2009. The new edit features a runtime vastly "tightened up" to 14 minutes, a new sound mix including 'Kayte Noise' (qv)' performance redubbed by 'Deirdre Yee' (qv) and an atmospheric use of ambient noise and redone color correction.

The character of Nicky, the ghost played by 'Lindsay Garrallo' (qv) was originally to be played by 'Charli Henley' (qv). She was conceptually inspired by the character "Oiwa-san" in the Japanese folktale Yotsuya Kaidan, one of J.L. Carrozza's favorite stories. In the story, originally performed as a Kabuki play, Oiwa was a woman whose treacherous husband poisoned and disfigured her so he could marry the younger daughter of a Lord to gain employment and status. On the night of Iuemon's wedding, Oiwa returns in spectral form and drives her former husband mad. The story has been filmed by numerous filmmakers in Japan from 'Nobuo Nakagawa (I)' (qv) to 'Kenji Misumi (I)' (qv) to 'Kinji Fukasaku' (qv) and Carrozza has always had interest in a version of the story as well.
The USA Today that Bobby reads was the edition printed on July 14, 1993. Even though Bobby says "Stocks are up!", the Dow Jones Industrial average was actually down about 9 points on July 13, 1993.

info: CONT: At the beginning, when Cory is Talking to Emily, there's a crowd of people behind Cory. In the next shot, is a few seconds later, the group is gone.

FACT: When Corey Banks references silicone on the periodic table, there is no such element. Silicone is a compound used in breast implants, while silicon is the element on the periodic table used in computer processors
DATE: As Khrishnah approaches the cemetery gate there is a 2003 Dodge Neon parked in the distance.

CONT: In the scene where the boys are siphoning gas out of the bully's car, there is a shot of the three bullies coming out of the front door of the house. One of them slips on the steps, but the camera cuts to another shot just before we would have seen what was going to be a MAJOR landing on his rear.
CONT: Gunther's shirt changes from when they leave their old house, to when they get to their new house.
CONT: As Gunther does his paper round, the weather changes between shots.
DATE: As Khrishnah approaches the cemetery gate there is a 2003 Dodge Neon parked in the distance.

FAKE: When the four are standing at the bridge and the woman fires a final round into the "zombie" on the ground, there is clearly another person standing behind the couple by the truck when there shouldn't be anybody.
CREW: When Jean, Kip and Claire are in the locker room, there's a point where you can see the marking tape "x" on the floor.

CONT: When Danyael jumps on the motorcycle he hits the gear pedal first, the we cut to see him pull the clutch lever. Since the motor is already running, punching in first gear without pull the clutch would cause the motor to die and the motorcycle to make an abrupt leap.
CONT: When Gabriel and Izzy are at the dry cleaners, the computer screen at first is a bright blue color, then the next scene it is a dark blue, almost black color.

FAKE: When Danyael is showing off for the kids with the chair, there's a shot of his head and neck. The collar of his shirt is lifted a couple of inches off his neck, obviously from the wire or harness he's using for that stunt.
MISC: Spelling mistake: an early scene in the movie takes place at St Gregory's Monastery, but the carved plaque at the building's front gate spells it "Monestary".
CONT: The real flower in the vase reappears after Abu takes it, then both flowers disappear a few shots later before Abu takes the other flower.

CONT: In the opening sequence, when Abu unloads the treasure off of the carpet, Aladdin says something to the effect of, "That's the last of it, Abu". In the subsequent shot, a bag of gold can be seen behind Abu.

CONT: When Aladdin and Jasmine make up in the palace garden (during Iago's song "Forget About Love"), Aladdin is wearing his "Ali Ababwa" prince clothes. When the we return to them after a scene with Jafar and Abis Mal, Aladdin and Jasmine are still in the palace garden, but Aladdin is suddenly wearing his "streetrat" clothes.
CONT: When Jasmine is being held prisoner in the dungeon by Jafar and Abis Mal, her legs are bound by a chain in one shot. In a later shot they are not.

CONT: During the dinner with the Sultan, the Genie cuts off his hand and it starts to tap dance. When it stops dancing, the Sultan's eyebrows are gone. Then when the Sultan starts laughing, his eyebrows return.
CONT: At the beginning of the movie, when Abis Mal puts the jeweled flower behind his belt, it changes sides between shots.

CONT: When Aladdin, Jasmine, and Genie are singing "Quite Like a Friend", at the end we see Aladdin on Genie's right side and Jasmine on the left, but in a later shot, it appears that Jasmine and Aladdin have switched places.

FAIR: SPOILER: After Genie saves Aladdin, he frees Carpet, Jasmine, Abu, and the Sultan. When he gets all four onto a roof of one of the palace towers, the Sultan's turban has reappeared after Jafar stole and slashed it earlier. Apparently, Genie restores it with his powers when he frees the others.

FAIR: SPOILER: Throughout the film, Genie is seen wearing his golden shackles, even though he was released from these shackles at the end of "Aladdin" when Aladdin wished him free. This is not an error, but a design decision (see trivia). Within the concept of the movie, the Genie must have conjured himself a new pair of shackles, possibly because he was so used wearing them for many thousands of years. In any case, given his powers, any discontinuity in Genie's appearance is explainable.

FAIR: During the song 'Nothing In The World', Genie tells Aladdin and Jasmine about his travels around the world. He mentions being at the pyramids at Giza in Egypt, but then in the same part the three are shown at the Temple of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel with the pyramids in the background, even though Giza is in the north of Egypt, while Abu Simbel is almost as far south as it's possible to go in Egypt. However, what we see is clearly not an actual location, but Genie's "virtual reality" where anything is possible. After all, the statues at Abu Simbel have Aladdin's and Jasmine's faces, indicating that it's all not exactly real.

CONT: When Aladdin is led to his execution, his wrists are chained in front of him. This continues all the way to when he is kneeling over the chopping block. When Genie swoops in to save him, his hands are now tied behind his back.

FAKE: When the four are standing at the bridge and the woman fires a final round into the "zombie" on the ground, there is clearly another person standing behind the couple by the truck when there shouldn't be anybody.
CREW: When Jean, Kip and Claire are in the locker room, there's a point where you can see the marking tape "x" on the floor.
CONT: When Fingers hands the baseball bat to Mac in the tunnel, he puts it in the hole handle end first. In the view from inside the tunnel the bat comes in fat end first.
CONT: When David is hitting all the foul balls, one hits and breaks a pot of flowers, but in the next shot the flower pot is back where it was.
SYNC: When The Great Fear throws Small's toy over the fence everybody is screaming, When it cuts to a different position they are still screaming but their mouths are closed.
FAKE: Obvious stunt double when the dog is chasing David into the junk yard.
FAKE: One of the missiles that Johnny launches lands on the roof of there club and knocks it in. But later it is as before.
FAKE: When David grabs his red rocket coat he tucks it under his shirt. When he is going on his bike it is still under his shirt but when he starts riding away it is in his back pocket
FAKE: When David is running out of the "fun house", his right sock is pulled up to his knee. Seconds later, the scar is showing and he is pulling up his sock from his ankle.
CREW: When Mr. Mertle's wall gets knocked over you can see two black wires that are obviously pulling it over.
DATE: As the model Space Shuttle flies over the city, it goes over a Foot Locker. The movie takes place in 1972, Foot Locker did not exist until 1974.

DATE: At the end of the movie, the narrator explains that Hayley grew up to be a supermodel and a pitcher on the Olympic softball team. Women's softball did not become an Olympic sport until 1996. Hayley would have been around 35 years old in 1996, a very unlikely age for an Olympic softball player.

DATE: The model of the space shuttle includes a rust colored external fuel tank. In the early flights of the space shuttle the tank was painted white. Most likely if any models existed during development of the shuttle they would have had the tank painted white.

CONT: When the Space Shuttle model takes off, it flies in a high arc away from the launch site like the real one, but when the boosters fall back down they fall right back down where they launched from.
DATE: David puts on shoes out of a box labeled Nike. Nike was established in the 1960s but not named Nike until 1978, six years after the movie is set.
FACT: Anastasia is repeatedly called a princess throughout the movie. This is untrue as she and her sisters would be known as Grand Duchesses.
FACT: Anastasia is shown to be at least 5-7 during the Russian Revolution. At the time she was actually 17 and 29 days old.
FACT: There is no mention of Anastasia's two older sisters, Maria and Olga.
FACT: Anastasia did not survive but in fact died with the rest of her family.
PLOT: SPOILER: There was no explanation on how Martin was reverted back into a normal mouse at the end of the movie.
CREW: When the witch has the first kid on the table there is a crouching man in the background as the camera moves up.
CONT: The scar that was burned into Taylor's wrist at the initiation is missing in later scenes when she's not wearing her watch.

FACT: Towards the end of the movie, Taylor Brooks dials 911 on a cell phone to allow the police to overhear Nathan Lloyd's plot, but she never presses the "send" button on the phone, so there is no way it would've connected to 911's service. You hear the beeps for 9-1-1, but no beep for send...

CONT: When Taylor is running and Ethan stops her for the "apology break" he drops his book bag off his shoulder to the ground and two shots later it's back on his shoulder but he never picked it back up and then in the next shot it's back off when he grabs her arm.
FAKE: When the mechanic gets out of the truck there are several buildings reflected in the window and on the side of the truck, despite the fact that the scene takes place miles away from town.
CONT: A dark coloured car is seen driving on the road behind the blonde standing by her car, but in the next shot there is no other car on the road.
CREW: Reflected in the cop's sunglasses.
DATE: At the beginning of the movie, supposedly set in 1949, the front door has a modern deadbolt in addition to the normal lock.
CREW: You can see the reflection of equipment when the cab pulls away after dropping Star at the B & B.

FAKE: Flopped shot: near the end of the film, when Harlan goes back alone, the first time he fires into the air, it's left-handed, with a left-handed bolt-action rifle. Subsequently, the rifle is right-handed and Harlan is right-handed.

CONT: When the bride zombie pops out of the washing machine and strangles the baking woman, the dead woman is not wearing socks, because you see her feet kicking as she dies. However, when the baking woman is stuffed in the washing machine she is wearing dark socks that you can see as her feet turn round and round and the zombies giggle!
FAKE: When Jeff and April find Chocolate, the dog, dead in the woods, the one short shot of the dog clearly shows that it is breathing.
CONT: When the scene changes between Zoe and Jeff while they talk on the phone, Zoe's hairstyle changes dramatically between the shots.

FAKE: Joshua, Jeff, and Zoe place mirrors on the front door in order to keep the zombies away from the house. Then moments after their dialogue, a camera shot from outside of the house reveals that the mirrors on the front door are now gone. Yet no zombies where ever seen removing them.
CHAR: When Zoe leaves a message for her brother Jeff, she writes "Leff" instead of "Jeff" in cursive.

GEOG: When the Westminster clock tower is destroyed, the Houses of Parliament and Parliament Square are nowhere to be seen. Instead, the Westminster clock tower is depicted as a free-standing tower on the riverbank. In actuality is part of the Parliament buildings.

FAKE: When the Writer is showing his wife the planet Mars, the bottom half of the frame is quite obviously bathed in hot summer sunshine, and yet the top half, depicting a matted-in CGI sky, is dark and filled with stars.

DATE: CGI shots of London do not in any way reflect the actual layout of the city itself; one re-occurring mistake is to show the city filled with Tudor cottages. Very few buildings of the this kind can be found in London as the entire city was destroyed by fire in 1666, prompting a rebuild utilizing only stone and brick.
FAKE: SPOILER: When the Writer and the Artillery Man are reunited towards the end of the film, a few shots reveal that the Writer's fake mustache is peeling off on one side.

DATE: Much of the Architecture in the street scenes of "London" is, in fact, American; Brownstones, typical of U.S. cities (and definitely not British ones), are seen throughout the film and the in the UK, lamp posts terminating in square lanterns and topped with a hood to reflect light down upon the street have always been favored over the American-style spherical lamps seen in the film.
DATE: Modern shop fronts, litter bins and chrome outdoor seating outside a coffee shop can be seen in 1890's "London" (actually Seattle).
CONT: Although in CGI long shots London is depicted as a Medieval city with dirt roads and gravel paths, in street scenes shot in Seattle clearly show the city as having concrete roads.
CONT: Throughout the film, Big Ben constantly reads 3:00, regardless of the actual time established elsewhere in any given scene.

FACT: The uniforms worn by the British troops in the film are not correct at all. Most of them appear to be cobbled together from mid to late 20th century USMC Alphas, and many of the other "soldiers" look more like Boer Commandos (right period, wrong country), or Franco's Phalangist/Fascist troops from the Spanish Civil War.
FACT: The Artilleryman is shown driving his gun team from the limber box. In reality, he would be riding one of the nearside wheel horses.
DATE: After the narrator flees the pit after the Martians' first attack, the train that passes in the background is a late 20th century Americal diesel model rather than a British steam locomotive.
FAKE: The Union Jack flag on the Thunderchild is shown blowing towards the wind as the ship speeds towards the Martian war machine instead of being blown back.
GEOG: The Artilleryman, supposedly an Englishman, uses the American pronunciation of "aluminum" as opposed to the English "aluminium".
GEOG: Parts of London such as Primrose Hill, which have been major urban centers for hundreds of years, are depicted in the film as being empty fields.
FAKE: The same extras are killed several times throughout the film.
DATE: People in modern dress can be seen in the far background during some of the street scenes.
MISC: The Writer looks through the observatory telescope with his closed eye.

CONT: After the massacre on the common, which happens at sundown, The Writer runs home. By the time he dives into a bush after being startled by a tradesman and his young helper, it is night but in the very next scene, taking place only a few minutes later, it is twilight and when he reaches home, it is suddenly day again.

FAKE: Some of the camera angles on the background plates do not match the angles of the foreground action in the blue screen shots. For example the view from The Writer's bedroom window gives the impression that the ground is at a 45 degree angle to the house, rather than 90 degrees as it should be. Also, whenever anyone is driving a cart, the backgrounds are so mismatched that grass and flowers appear to be over 8 feet tall.

MISC: It is evident that, during the "Thunderchild" scenes, that CGI ships have been layered over stock footage of the sea shot from an aeroplane. The result is that the sea appears to be moving sideways rapidly, not in accordance with the direction that the ships are traveling.

DATE: The guns on the Thunderchild appear to be AA guns, and appear to fire even though unmanned. There were no AA guns in Victorian times, largely because powered flight was not achieved until the early 20th century.
FACT: The Scientist tells the writer early in the movie that Mars is 40 million miles closer to the Sun than the Earth is. Earth is closer to the Sun than Mars is.

FACT: Human skeletons cannot continue to move once all the soft tissue is gone from a human body. Yet, multiple times the skeletons of people killed by the heat rays thrash around for several seconds after only the bones are left.
CONT: When the teenage girl is taken by the witch, she first removes the apple from her mouth, but in the next scene where the girl is on the grinder table, the apple is back in place.

CONT: When Max and his brother are attempting to escape from the Witch's basement, they work together to knock down a door. As they throw themselves against it it's a single door, but when they come through the other side it's a double door.
BOOM: The shadow of the boom mic is visible on the walls many times throughout the movie.
FAKE: SPOILER: When the zombie bites the black girl's arm, there's blood on her arm before she's bitten. Furthermore, the arm is white (caucasian) and the girl is black.
FAKE: SPOILER: When Teufel bites Gus at the end of the film, he is about six inches away from his neck and not actually making contact with him.
CONT: Theodore Rex's shoes change from red to blue and back throughout the movie.

CONT: SPOILER: After Ted is shot in his left arm, Katie tries to convince him he doesn't need a gun. As she does, the position of the gun changes between front and rear shots. Katie sways slightly in rear shots, but is motionless in front shots.
SYNC: When Katie talks to Theodore about his breath, it's a very obvious voice-over that doesn't fit at all.
CREW: When the Guy in a Bag calls out to the caterpillar, it rises up. The puppet operator's hand is clearly visible in the first shot, lifting it from underneath the table.
CONT: When Master Little tosses Van on the mat, he lands on a thick red one. When he gets up however he is on a thin blue mat.
SYNC: At the end of the film, there are no women present besides Thumbelina herself. However, we can hear female voices cheering the prince.
FACT: The name of fairy tale author, Hans Christian Andersen is spelled incorrectly at the beginning of the film as "Anderson".
FACT: A calendar shows that April 17, 2011 is a Saturday. It is actually Palm Sunday.
CONT: Lewis is being questioned by Detective Becker after the incident at his house, Becker's gloves change from being on to off in each scene.

FACT: On the chess board shown at the beginning (and then again later in the movie) the main character promotes the pawn to a knight which both he and the computer claim is a checkmate for black. It isn't a checkmate, since white can then take the knight with the bishop. There is a mate in three for black (rook to g2, white is forced to move the king into the corner, rook to a1, white is forced to interpose the bishop, rook takes bishop = checkmate)

CHAR: When reciting the contents of the cabinet on the wall to the Doctor, Clay says he is reading "top to bottom, left to right", but the six bottles of peroxide he mentions last of the things he recites are in the top left corner.

FAKE: (at around 1 min) As the initial wave hits the Titanic II, everyone in the dining room is tossed all around with arms flailing, not only do glasses and dishes not move, but the wine inside of the glasses does not move either.

The 2004 series has Kanzaki's plot foiled, and Shin opts not to desert, deciding to stay at Area 88 and eventually earn his way home - ending on an optimistic note.

Screenwriter 'Joe Halpin (II)' (qv) is quoted in the book "Seagalogy: The Ass Kicking Films of Steven Seagal" as saying that "Attack Force" had originally been written and filmed as "Harvester," a sci-fi/horror movie with 'Steven Seagal (I)' (qv) and his men battling an invading force of vampire space aliens. After Seagal, Halpin and director 'Michael Keusch' (qv) had delivered the finished sci-fi film, the production and distribution company decided to eliminate the sci-fi space-alien elements and replace them with another plot about a super-addictive drug that turns its users into superhuman killers. They called back a few of the lower-paid actors for re-shoots, re-dubbed the majority of Seagal's dialog via ADR, totally re-edited the film and changed it into "Attack Force" as it is now known. Seagal and Halpin were not involved.

Hurricane Isabelle hit Middlesex Virginia two days after shooting, leaving the cast and crew with no power or running water for three weeks. Brainiac's source material is a 1962 horror movie called _El barón del terror (1962)_ (qv), one of dozens of low budget Mexican monster films trucked over the border and sloppily re-dubbed by schlock purveyor 'K. Gordon Murray' (qv). The Brainiac original Spanish language title features a suave, meteor-riding monster exacting revenge on the descendants of the Mexican Inquisition by sucking their brains out. Murray produced more than 40 films between the late 50s and mid 70s. The new Brainiac began a few years ago as a backyard homage to its namesake. At the time, King was managing a film production lighting house and working on documentaries and shorts on the side.

In the spring of 2003, Terry Michael King and 'Greg Bayan' (qv) went to a horror convention in Cleveland to find out how plausible it was to procure a Brainiac monster. Greg asked makeup-and-effects legend 'Tom Savini' (qv) for help. Savini agreed, utilizing students Allison Amann and 'James Woodruff (I)' (qv) from his Special Make-up Effects Program at the Douglas Education Center in Monessen, Pennsylvania.

The Brainiac team drew up an extensive monster wish list design reminiscent of the photogenic mutants that held audiences captive in the 50s and 60s. They wanted it to have bat-like features and the brain exposed with pulsating brain lobes. They also wanted a phallic, brain-sucking tongue that attached to its victims heads like a leech. And deformed, meaty claws.

The writers had originally planned to adhere to the original Brainiac premise, but found the demands of staging a 17th century Inquisition/Trial scene too overwhelming. With a simpler setting in mind, Greg and 'Matthew J. Bayan' (qv) spent two weeks revamping the script with a modern pretext. Addiction drives their monster to brain-slurping, rather than the occult.
The movie's connection with 'Tom Savini' (qv) has created quite a bit of buzz in the horror community, including a recent "Fangoria" feature article.

'Brian De Palma' (qv)'s _Carlito's Way (1993)_ (qv) took the first books title because at the time it was decided that they would not take the title of the second book "After Hours" to avoid confusion with the 'Martin Scorsese' (qv) -directed movie of the same name (_After Hours (1985)_ (qv)).

When Harry says "So he plays Dungeons and Dragons" refers to the role-playing game (formerly by TSR) that director 'Chris Thompson (XXXIV)' (qv) and producer 'Stan Wankowski' (qv) have both played since the late 70's. The shot from inside the trunk was an homage to director 'Quentin Tarantino (I)' (qv), who uses the shot in all of his films.
The characters Harry Stanton and Dean Jessup were named after 'Harry Dean Stanton' (qv), an actor from _Alien (1979)_ (qv), one of the director's favorite films.
The castle used in the film is an actual Italian castle owned by the president of Full Moon Pictures, the distribution company.

The original screenplay was called Bloody Mary. The title was cleared in every territory except Japan, where the name Bloody Mary is copyrighted, and it was suggested that the title be changed to Dead Mary for release in that country alone. When the film's producers discovered that another film, also called Bloody Mary, was being readied for release around the same time, it was decided that the film's title be officially changed to Dead Mary in order to avoid confusion. This spawned an inside joke in the finished film, when the better-known game Bloody Mary is dismissed as being "the lame version" of Dead Mary.

The script originally featured an actual Bloody Mary who, when summoned by the mirror game, rose from the depths of the lake to murder the characters one by one. Director Robert Wilson decided that it would be more interesting if the evil force was never seen, but instead could manifest itself in any one of the old friends gathered at the cabin, thus making the film more a creepy paranoia piece and less a supernatural slasher film. However, many film websites still make reference to the film's original (and now incorrect) synopsis.

When a group of alien agents from a dying planet come to Earth under the leadership of Isis to build a portal to connect both worlds, the warrior Rykker opposes the invaders and defends the earthlings. He rescues the teenager Julie, whose family was murdered by the invaders, and together they try to destroy the portal and avoid the invasion commanded by the cruel Saylon.
note: Claudio Carvalho, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

info: Rykker is an intergalactic warrior trapped on Earth, destined to fight a gang of ruthless aliens known as The Syndicate. The syndicate is an alien fifth column plotting to take over the world. The film opens with a spectacular highway chase, as Rykker liquidates several syndicate agents. Saylon is a top syndicate leader who comes from outer space and crash-lands on Earth. His mission: to build a wormhole link between Earth and the alien planet - a portal - making possible a full-scale invasion of the Earth. Isis is the sexy and ruthless leader of the syndicate on Earth. While launching a robbery spree to steal the spare parts necessary to build the portal, Isis becomes hell bent on destroying Rykker and clearing the way for Saylon's master plan. Julie is a fifteen year old whose family is murdered during the hijacking of a truck carrying material for the portal. Julie, left totally alone in the world, seeks vengeance on the killers. Rykker also seeks to find them. He must stop them before they complete the portal and flood the world with alien scum. Julie and Rykker are thrown together by tragic circumstance. They hook up - actually, she follows him against his will; he tries and tries to ditch her, but she keeps popping up, even saving his life at one point - and embark on a cross country journey, with Isis and an army of syndicate killers in hot pursuit. The final showdown, inside a nuclear reactor, is an intense action climax, as Rykker and Julie battle Isis, Saylon and their army of killers, and try to prevent the portal from opening a rein of destruction upon Earth.

They're here and living among us! Filmmaker J.J. Barmettler and controversial UFO Investigator Brandon Scott have captured the UFO subculture from the inside out working 43 artists, 23 abduction victims, 30 experts and 200 eye witnesses who have all had experiences in the chilling UFO Alien phenomenon. Their discovery shows that there is a hidden generation of alien/human hybrids living among us. In the process of the investigation a female hybrid speaks out to the public for the first time ever caught on film. This "hybrid" narrative/documentary film weaves story and fact in an epic portrayal of one man's fight for free will and his drive to save humanity.

A clever send up of the UFO genre based on Brandon Scott's real life escapades as he explores the UFO subculture with a biting edge and wit. Brandon Plays a parody of himself which takes us on a wild ride that at times seems like a cross between X-Files and Spinal Tap. Follow Brandon as he cleverly navigates his way through the world of UFO Abductees and Alien/Human Hybrids while dogging a shadow government agent bent on stopping his findings. This offbeat mockumentary is sprinkled with real life people from the UFO community; from Budd Hopkins to Dr. J.J. Hurtak and actual people claiming to be abductees and alien/human hybrids. What is real and what is illusion? See the film and find out.

In a galaxy far away, alien criminals organize a spectacular prison break. Pursued by their home planet's authorities, their leader Zin decides there's one place to go: through a wormhole that allows instantaneous travel to Earth. Cole is the Alien tracker who's in hot pursuit of the escaped convicts. when a government group investigating extraterrestrials captures one, Cole must break into the facility and free him before they gather the hard evidence they need to prove that Alien life exists on earth.

A suspected prisoner uprising brings Marines to the prison planet of Rove 12, but nothing is what it seems. The few surviving prisoners are hiding from a ruthless, blood thirsty creature. Now the prisoners and the marines must fight together to get off the planet ALIVE!

Sara and Tom Johnson are two very bored teenagers. But that's all about to change. During a family vacation to an old western ghost town, the bickering siblings stumble upon a portal which catapults them back in time to the old west.

Explores the stories of three unconventional dads who reveal their own personal journeys into fatherhood. Mike, who became a father for the fifth time at the age of 71 years; Johnny, a gay father and Roddy, who endured the seemingly endless frustrations and emotions of the IVF process before eventually becoming an adoptive father of a six month year old baby boy. This film will make us question what the role of the modern father really represents. Hand drawn animations are used to bring memories to life and perfectly frame both the joys and frustrations of fatherhood. This film is a timely examination of how ordinary people react to change when the want for children and family becomes a vital decision in their life.

All About US is an interesting foray into the thinking and the technology that lies behind the most popular tracks from Peter Gabriel's US album. It contains documentary coverage of the thinking behind the most popular music videos together with the actual music videos themselves. Music videos include:1. Digging In the Dirt 2. Steam 3. Blood of Eden 4. Solsbury Hill 5. Zaar 6. Come Talk to Me 7. Kiss That Frog. Directed by Michael Coulson, All About Us includes rare interviews and behind the scenes footage of Gabriel as he finishes his album and gets his haircut ready to go out on tour. It also features some of the 11 contemporary artists who were commissioned by Gabriel, in an innovative approach to marketing, to create works inspired by the songs. Each of the artists - Andy Goldsworthy, Yayoi Kusama, David Mach, Helen Chadwick, Zadok Ben-David, Zush, Rebecca Horn, Mickael Beth- Selassie , Ian Hughes, Jordan Baseman, Finbar Kelly and Bili Bidjocka were given a track as inspiration. Coulson recorded their creative process. Seeing the way that Gabriel has merged the artistic concepts of both his music, lyric, and the artistic interpretations into the completed music videos demonstrates the multi-layered meaning and message of his works.

October 31st begins like any other day. Adults go to work. Children go to school. But when night falls, the real party begins. That's when a young group of friends get together to tell some of the most twisted and terrifying stories imaginable. But as their stories begin to unfold, an unexpected dark side to their personalities is revealed...

Self-mutilation. Anorexia. Binge drinking. Despair. Unseen cries of desperation behind closed doors. Yet, this music video speaks of the yearning of One who wants more for those who hurt. "All I Want" is a moving look at the struggles of the human heart to find love and the surprising One who waits to offer the solace we so desperately seek.

ALL JAMS ON DECK is a 96-minute film about blues jamming. Featured are performances by such major musical artists as Tommy Castro, Elvin Bishop, Marcia Ball, Kim Wilson, Johnny and Edgar Winter, Commander Cody, Larry McCray, Lee Oskar, Coco Montoya, Rick Estrin, Sista Monica Parker, Jimmy Thackery, John Nemeth, Steve Berlin, Vasti Jackson, Leon Blue, and more. Also included are discussions of the history, techniques and etiquette of jamming featuring the artists themselves, as well as SiriusXM Radio's Bill Wax and music historian and producer Bob Porter. The film was produced by veteran music filmmaker Robert Mugge and his partner Diana Zelman, executive produced by Roger Naber, and shot on the October 2010 Legendary Rhythm & Blues Cruise from San Diego to the Mexican Riviera.

Back in the day, "Dub Ridaz" was one of the hottest crews in Hip-Hop, but the days of platinum records, sold-out shows and fly females are nothing but a memory. Now with no record deal and fading skills, they're forced to make a living flipping burgers and working other dead-end jobs. But Chances, the leader of the crew, and his boys are fed up and ready to get back in the game. Hooking up with a new record label that hatches a wild publicity stunt to promote the new Dub Ridaz album, it's a race against the clock for the group to pull off the PR scheme, pay back an old debt and make a hit record. The stakes are high, the odds are against them and all lies are on the Dub Ridaz in this hilarious Hip-Hop comedy!

A documentary look at the people of the Hope House Foundation in Norfolk, Virginia who have put forth a simple premise for thinking about - and helping to enhance - the quality of the lives of those who are developmentally disabled. It is that a life of one's own to live to the best of one's ability and with the respect of others, is a human right, and a responsibility for all of us.

'All That Remains' is a powerful story of a WW2 veteran with dementia, suffering a confused world of his life's painful losses with Death his only companion. To end his misery, he strikes a deal with Death, discovering both Death has no master ...and his own salvation.

ALL THE LONELY PEOPLE documents the journey of Ben Anderson, a 25 year-old musician with Asperger's Syndrome, as he attends a program for Autistic adults designed to help him learn to navigate and make sense of the social world that has eluded him his entire life. This intimate portrait gives a sense of the great isolation and confusion Ben and many adults on the Autism Spectrum feel and examines the question: what happens when kids with autism grow up?

All American Murder is the story of Artie. He is the new guy on Campus and he only has one thing on his mind, Tally Fuller. Tally is the most popular girl in school, until she is found dead and Artie becomes the prime suspect! Will he be able to clear his name and find the real killer, only time will tell.

While saving the crew of the first manned mission to the sun, Superman is poisoned by solar radiation. Dying, he decides to fulfill his lifelong dreams, while still saving the Earth from various threats. But when Lex Luthor reveals his latest plot to control the world, Superman must use his remaining strength to stop him.

Elvis impersonators now number more than 35,000 worldwide. Almost Elvis investigates this cultural phenomenon with humor and insight. Filmed all over America, it traces the journeys of several hopefuls to the world's largest Elvis impersonator contest and documents their quest to create the perfect illusion of the King of Rock'n'Roll.

Be captured by the Invisible. To ease the weight of their college workload, unsuspecting teenagers seize the opportunity to to turn their end-of-the-summer party into a sick house wrecking. What happens instead they will never forget. In a classic tale of one girl learning to break free of the past, Almost Invisible has captured the attention of Washington DC Mid-Atlantic teenagers and aspiring filmmakers alike. Seamless special effects, a haunting original soundtrack. Almost Invisible. It's almost here.

A sex farce about a woman with an infertile husband who is desperate to get pregnant. She enlists the help of her neighbor and an in-law. Meanwhile her husband begins an affair with the neighbor's wife.

While the Chipmunks are working at the amusement park, Majestic Movie Studios, in a singing attraction. Little do they know that the real Dr. Frankenstein are in a new attraction called, "Frankenstein's Castle". After Alvin drives a crazy bus ride, they miss their next performance and get locked in the park after closing time. Dr. Frankenstein figures that the castle isn't scary enough and re-creates the real Frankenstein and after the monster finds the boys, it starts a wild and wacky adventure!

It's the Chipmunks' third and final full-length feature! Alvin is struggling with nightmares of werewolves. Alvin believes that the new next-door neighbor Mr. Talbot is a werewolf. Of course, no one believes him. Meanwhile, the boys are working on the school production of Dr. Jekyll & Mr. Hyde. When Alvin blows up the school auditorium, he is expelled from the production. Theodore is put in to rise his lack of confidence. Alvin and Simon are trying to discover the secret of Mr. Talbot. Will the play go as planned or will the Chipmunks mess it up?! And is Mr. Talbot a werewolf?

Baron Dixon has been teased his whole life. He believes, with all his heart, that he really is an alien and that he will soon be leaving Planet Earth. His two best friends - a couple of doped-up, gun loving, outcast hillbillies-believe in Baron. His beautiful girlfriend wants to believe him, but Baron is just too crazy! Soon, they discover that even the impossible is possible and that aliens really do exist!

After Jesse James is wounded by a bullet to the chest, Frank James splits the gang up and plans a rendezvous in four days time. With U.S.-Marshall Kane in hot pursuit, and betrayal within the outlaw band, the stage is set for a blazing and climactic shootout in the deserted town of 'Gila Wells'.

A young smalltown reporter, Jessie St. Claire, begins investigating a killer stalking his victims making video tapes. This might just be the career opportunity, which she has hoped for. When she herself becomes a target and suddenly disappears, the case attracts a colleague from the nationally syndicated television show "American Crime" as well. Together with Jessie's camera-man and later joined by her producer he tries to solve the mysterious case.

The crew of a television of a small town composed of the reporter Jesse St. Claire, her lesbian supervisor Jane Berger and the intern cameraman Rob Latrobe are investigating the disappearance of the stripper Diana Cox. Rob received a videotape and found the shooting of another woman, Linda Mitchell, in the same video, and he is convinced that the killer stalked his victims while filming them. When Jesse vanishes without a trace, the reporter Albert Bodine from the syndicated television show "American Crime" joins the team in their investigation.
note: Claudio Carvalho, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

info: American Herro is the remarkable story of a young Kurdish girl who comes to America as a refugee from Iraq and lives out the American dream. 30-years later, traveling the globe working for Condoleeza Rice, U.S. Diplomat Herro Mustafa invites her first American friend, filmmaker Kirk Roos, to visit Iraq and retrace her steps to freedom.

American Herro is a documentary about a rare, lifetime friendship that bridges two cultures together. This is the story of a young girl, Herro Mustafa from Kurdistan, Iraq and a young boy from North Dakota, U.S.A. Two destined friends, worlds apart, brought together through the beginnings of a genocide brought on by Saddam Hussein and his counterparts. The conflict beginning in her homeland, Iraq, targeting the Kurds, caused young Herro and her family to flee to safety in America. Specifically, her family landed in Minot, ND, the hometown of filmmaker Kirk Roos. 30-years later, Herro now works as Secretary of State Condoleeza Rice's Special Advisor to the Middle East. In July, 2007, Herro and Kirk, along with their respective families traveled to Kurdistan, Iraq. They RETRACED the steps of The Mustafa's family escape through the mountains of Kurdistan into Iran, where they lived in a refugee camp for two years. They met Herro's long-lost extended family, cousins and explored the comparisons and contrasts of Kurdish struggle, home and abroad. With beautiful footage from Kurdistan and intimate scenes from family and friend, the film paints a portrait of a real "hero," and a real American.

"American High School," a romantic comedy, is centered on two people who marry young and contend with the consequences of "bad" actions. Moreover, it is a story about a young, frightened girl, Gwen Adams who tries to break away from her father, find peace with her husband, and find peace within. In a world that expects everything from her, being herself was the last thing on her mind. When pushed to the breaking point, she discovers her own self-worth. But is it too late?

Small lives begin at the end of high school for this surreal society. A senior who married young must contend with her life, love, and pursuit of individuality and femininity in a narcissistic, misogynistic world of irony. Gwen Adams, her husband Holden, and school rival Hilary complete the love triangle as Principal Mann makes their lives living hell. Also featuring Miss Apple and Johnny Awesome. Life isn't simple wrapped in a bow -- there are bumps, bruises, and broken hearts. Through tears are laughter, and in the transition to maturity, boys and girls find themselves through each other.

Ten years after the first American Pie movie, three new hapless virgins discover the Bible hidden in the school library at East Great Falls High. Unfortunately for them, the book is ruined, and with incomplete advice, the Bible leads them on a hilarious journey to lose their virginity.

Rachael Newman has developed an interest for murders after she met psycho Patrick Bateman. To further study the subject, she enrolls at the university department for Behavioural and Social Sciences, under the expert leadership of ex-FBI man Robert Starkman. Very certain about herself, Rachael has one single goal: to become class assistant. It's a prestigious job as having that position will almost guarantee employment at the FBI. But becoming class assistant is no easy task to accomplish, as the first trouble arises when secretary Gerty Fleck decides she is too young for it. And Gerty Fleck won't be the only obstacle.

With only a few hours to go on the final leg of their Ohio tour, the Little Devils find themselves stranded in a no-name town. Tim, Jeff, Rick and Ben pass the hours waiting for their van to be repaired by revealing a little more about themselves through true, yet unbelievable stories.

Ameere has finally proposed to his long time love Jacquelyne, and that day of marital bliss is fast approaching. Only two things stand in the way of Ameere marrying the woman that he truly loves. A wild bachelor party, and a deep seeded secret between the two of them.

Amira (Kaitlyn Terrill), an aspiring singer with big hopes and dreams, attempts to find her way to stardom. Upon hearing about an open casting call for a club in New York, she auditions for the owner. After the audition goes sour, she finds herself derailed from the path of her dreams. Luckily with encouragement from the provocative and much adored headlining singer of the club (Luke Yellin), she finds the strength to take a chance and sing.

An investigation into the grassroots campaign and unprecedented Internet strategy that combined to vault President Obama into the White House. Ffeaturing interviews with leading activists, artists, analysts, journalists, civil rights leaders and insiders.

In a final and epic battle in the thrilling sequel to the now classic "Barbarian Queen", Althalia, leads a revolt of peasants and female warriors against the wicked ruler, Arkaris, to regain her throne.

Barbie plays Rosella in this new musical film. Shipwrecked as a child, Rosella grows up on the island under the watchful eyes of her loving animal friends. The arrival of Prince Antonio leads Rosella and her furry pals to explore civilization and ultimately save the kingdom by uncovering a secret plot.

In her first animated musical featuring seven original songs, Barbie comes to life in this modern re-telling of a classic tale of mistaken identity and the power of friendship. Based on the story by Mark Twain, Barbie as The Princess and The Pauper features Barbie in an exciting dual role as a princess and a poor village girl - two girls who look amazingly alike. The girls' paths are fated to cross when Princess Anneliese is captured and Erika, her look-alike, must try to save her. Can Erika pretend to be the Princess and foil her captor, the evil Preminger? And what of the handsome King Dominick, who falls in love with Erika, mistaking her for Princess Anneliese? In this magical musical performance, two beautiful, adventurous girls dare to follow their dreams and discover that destiny is written in a very special place: your heart.

Elina goes to a fairy school to learn dancing and fairy magic. The spring of the fairy land is soon threatened by evil Laverna who intends to prevent fairies from performing the annual vital rainbow dance. Elina must stop quarreling with her fellow students and unite them to save the first bud of the spring.

Barbie returns in Mermaid Tale 2 as the beautiful surfing mermaid, Merliah Summers. Merliah is going to Australia for the ultimate surfing competition with her friends both human and sea. Things are looking up for Merliah until the evil mermaid Eris returns to try and take over the throne again. Its up to Merliah to stop Eris and save the beautiful mer-world of Oceana. As Merliah races the clock to save her mothers kingdom and finish the big surfing competition , Merliah learns anything is possible and that her love for both worlds land and sea are what brings out the best. Kelly Sheridan is back as the voice of the beautiful surfing Princess Merliah Summers.

A member of the royal family has to go to 'Aqualia' every 20 years to perform the 'Change of the Tides' ritual. Merliah, princess of Oceana, is a surfer and has the biggest heat of her life which clashes with the day of the ritual. However, when Calissa's (Merliah's mother AKA Queen of Oceana) sister 'Eris' escapes with a motive to take over Oceana, it's up to Merliah and her newly made friend to save Oceana, complete the ritual and by doing so get the power of making Meriliah.

King Randolph sends for his cousin Duchess Rowena to help turn his daughters, Princess Genevieve and her 11 sisters, into better ladies. But the Duchess takes away all the sisters fun, including the sisters favorite pastime: dancing.
